title: Quantum Computing Roadmap Signals Effort On Error Correction
excerpt: The Quantum Subcommittee of the U.S. Office of Science Advisory Committee described quantum computing as approaching an “inflection point” and proposed a roadmap toward scientifically useful, error-corrected quantum computing by 2028.
content:
Germany’s BSI advising against the use of the ISO-standardized Classic McEliece in new developments this September emphasises a rapidly shifting landscape in post-quantum cryptography. The November 2026 Quantum Briefing, published in collaboration with the Global Risk Institute, warns organizations that delaying migration to post-quantum cryptography based on waiting for a definitive arrival date for a cryptographically relevant quantum computer could prove too late.

“Organizations that wait for a precise date may find the time remaining shorter than what’s needed to complete the work ahead,” the report cautions, as even newly standardized algorithms face swift re-evaluation. This assessment follows the withdrawal of the HAWK candidate post-quantum signature scheme due to vulnerabilities uncovered by AI-assisted classical cryptanalysis, demonstrating that even new cryptographic algorithms aren’t immune to immediate flaws.

AI Impacts Quantum Computing and Cryptanalysis

Investment in fault-tolerant quantum computing is accelerating, with developers and governments focusing on scalability, manufacturing, error correction and system integration. The U.S. Office of Science Advisory Committee described quantum computing as approaching an “inflection point” in September 2026, proposing a roadmap toward scientifically useful, error-corrected quantum computing by 2028. The briefing emphasizes that building a resilient cryptographic posture requires agility, defense in depth and diversity, rather than a simple algorithm swap, and that organizations should also assess business continuity plans for outages caused by AI-enabled attackers exploiting cryptographic vulnerabilities.

Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Approaches Inflection Point

Resource estimates further support this trend, with one IonQ study suggesting a fault-tolerant trapped-ion machine with approximately 19,400 physical qubits could recover a private key on a widely used elliptic curve in roughly 26 days per attempt. Investment is now heavily focused on overcoming the most significant hurdles to achieving fault tolerance, including scalability, manufacturing challenges and robust error correction techniques.

These efforts reflect a recognition that future quantum computers will be specialized machines, designed for specific tasks rather than general-purpose computation. The convergence of advances in quantum hardware operations, driven by artificial intelligence, with the ability of AI-assisted classical cryptanalysis to expose vulnerabilities in even new algorithms, like the recently withdrawn HAWK candidate post-quantum signature scheme, creates a complex and evolving threat landscape.

Federal Deadlines Drive Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration

Federal deadlines are now intensifying the push for cryptography migration, spurred by recent findings that highlight the evolving nature of the quantum threat. The government’s mandate for federal agencies to adopt key establishment by December 31, 2030, and digital signatures by December 31, 2031, creates a firm timeline for action.

These dates are not arbitrary; they reflect an assessment that the years-long process of cryptographic migration may be compressed by accelerating developments in quantum computing. Similarly, despite ISO standardization in June 2026, Germany’s BSI advised against using Classic McEliece in new developments in September 2026, illustrating the rapid pace at which algorithms are being re-evaluated. The figure rests on IonQ’s assumptions about its own future hardware, and no existing machine can run the attack.
